ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Portal hypertension: 1

A patient with cirrhosis presents with hematemesis. Endoscopy shows dilated veins at the distal esophagus. Which portal-hypertension complication explains the bleeding source through collateral venous channels connecting portal and systemic circulations?

  1. Portosystemic shunting contributing to encephalopathy
  2. Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices
  3. Congestive splenomegaly and sequestration
  4. Portal-hypertensive ascites
  5. Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals
Answer and explanation

Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices

Elevated portal pressure can dilate collateral veins and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Option explanations

Portosystemic gastroesophageal varices: Elevated portal pressure can dilate collateral veins and cause life-threatening upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Congestive splenomegaly and sequestration: Portal hypertension can enlarge the spleen and contribute to thrombocytopenia. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Portal-hypertensive ascites: Portal pressure and sodium-retaining responses contribute to ascites. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Abdominal wall portosystemic collaterals: Dilated periumbilical veins can reflect collateral flow in portal hypertension. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Portosystemic shunting contributing to encephalopathy: Blood bypassing hepatic clearance can contribute to encephalopathy, including after TIPS. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
